terms.definition: An AWS Platform as a Service (PaaS) that automatically handles deployment, capacity provisioning, load balancing, auto-scaling, and health monitoring of web applications. You upload code; AWS handles the infrastructure.
terms.example: Like a smart building manager — you move in with your belongings (code) and the manager handles electricity, plumbing, and maintenance (EC2, ELB, CloudWatch).

terms.definition: A cloud service model where the provider manages the underlying infrastructure (servers, OS, runtime) and you only manage the application and data. Elastic Beanstalk is AWS's primary PaaS offering.
terms.example: PaaS is between IaaS (you manage EC2) and SaaS (you just use software like Gmail). With PaaS, you focus purely on writing code.

terms.definition: A logical container in Elastic Beanstalk that holds all versions of your code (application versions) and all environments that run those versions. Think of it like a GitHub repository.
terms.example: You create one Application called 'MyWebApp' and inside it you have three Environments: Dev, Test, and Production.

terms.definition: The actual running deployment of your application in Elastic Beanstalk. It contains real AWS resources: EC2 instances, security groups, load balancer, auto scaling group, and more.
terms.example: MyWebApp-Production is an environment — it has 3 EC2 instances behind a load balancer and serves real user traffic.

terms.definition: An Elastic Beanstalk environment type that handles incoming HTTP/HTTPS requests from users. This is the standard environment type for websites and REST APIs.
terms.example: A shopping website that handles user browsing and checkout requests runs in a Web Server environment.

terms.definition: An Elastic Beanstalk environment type that processes background tasks pulled from an Amazon SQS queue. Used for long-running or asynchronous workloads.
terms.example: A video transcoding service that processes uploaded videos in the background uses a Worker environment connected to SQS.

terms.definition: An Elastic Beanstalk deployment strategy that updates all instances simultaneously. It is the fastest but causes a brief period of downtime during the update.
terms.example: Good for development environments where a few minutes of downtime is acceptable. Never use in production.

terms.definition: An Elastic Beanstalk deployment strategy that updates instances in batches. Some instances serve the old version while others receive the new version, maintaining availability.
terms.example: With 4 instances and batch size 2: first update instances 1-2 (old 3-4 still serve traffic), then update 3-4. No downtime.

terms.definition: An Elastic Beanstalk deployment strategy that creates an entirely new set of instances with the new version. Only after passing health checks are the old instances terminated. Safest strategy with instant rollback.
terms.example: If the new version fails health checks, just terminate the new instances — old ones were never touched and continue serving traffic.

terms.definition: A deployment approach where two identical environments (Blue=current, Green=new) run simultaneously. Traffic is shifted by swapping CNAME URLs, enabling zero-downtime releases and instant rollback.
terms.example: Blue environment serves users now. Deploy new version to Green, test it. Swap CNAMEs — users now hit Green. If broken, swap back to Blue instantly.

terms.definition: The AWS infrastructure-as-code service that Elastic Beanstalk uses internally to provision all resources in an environment. A CloudFormation stack is created for each Beanstalk environment.
terms.example: When you create a Beanstalk environment, you can see a stack named awseb-e-XXXXXXXX in the CloudFormation console containing all your resources.

terms.definition: A color-coded status indicator in Elastic Beanstalk showing the overall state of an environment: Green (Ok), Yellow (Warning), Red (Degraded/Severe), or Grey (Pending/No data).
terms.example: A newly created environment shows Grey while launching, transitions to Green once the application is deployed and passing health checks.

terms.definition: Every version of code you upload to Elastic Beanstalk is stored as an Application Version in an automatically created S3 bucket. These persist even after environment termination.
terms.example: If you deploy 10 versions of your app over time, all 10 ZIP files are stored in the Beanstalk S3 bucket — you can roll back to any of them.

terms.definition: A directory placed inside your application ZIP file containing YAML or JSON configuration files. These files allow you to customize the Elastic Beanstalk environment: install packages, run commands, configure OS settings.
terms.example: Add .ebextensions/nginx.config to modify Nginx timeout settings, or .ebextensions/packages.config to install additional Linux packages on the EC2 instance.

terms.definition: A fully managed load balancer that distributes incoming traffic across multiple EC2 instances. Elastic Beanstalk creates one automatically for Load Balanced environments. Not free tier eligible.
terms.example: With 3 EC2 instances behind an ELB, if one instance becomes unhealthy, the ELB stops sending traffic to it automatically and your users see no disruption.

terms.definition: An AWS feature that automatically adjusts the number of EC2 instances based on load. Elastic Beanstalk configures an ASG for Load Balanced environments, scaling out when traffic increases and in when traffic drops.
terms.example: If you set min=2, max=10, scale out at 70% CPU: when traffic spikes, ASG adds instances up to 10; during quiet hours it scales back to 2.

terms.definition: An Elastic Beanstalk environment type with exactly one EC2 instance and no load balancer. Cost-effective and free-tier eligible. Suitable for development, testing, and low-traffic applications.
terms.example: A personal portfolio website with light traffic runs perfectly on a single t3.micro instance — no need for a load balancer or auto scaling.

terms.definition: Elastic Beanstalk itself has no additional charge. You pay only for the AWS resources the environment uses: EC2 instances, EBS storage, RDS, ELB, S3 storage, and data transfer.
terms.example: A single-instance environment with a t3.micro EC2 and 10 GB EBS: free tier eligible for the first 12 months of a new account.

terms.definition: The process of shutting down and deleting all AWS resources in an Elastic Beanstalk environment. Always done via the Beanstalk console — never by deleting the CloudFormation stack directly. S3 buckets are NOT deleted.
terms.example: After your lab or project is done, go to Environment → Actions → Terminate Environment, then manually delete the S3 bucket named elasticbeanstalk-[region]-[account-id].

terms.definition: Key-value pairs configured in the Elastic Beanstalk console that are passed to your application as environment variables at runtime. Used to securely provide database credentials, API keys, and configuration without hard-coding.
terms.example: Set DB_HOST=mydb.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com and DB_PASSWORD=secret123 in Beanstalk env vars. Your app reads them via os.environ['DB_HOST'] — credentials never touch source code.
